- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.33) over recent days, model tends to overestimate; reduce forecast by 2–5% for next period.
- After a sharp price spike (forecast > 85), model often overshoots and fails to correct; cap forecast at +10% above peak or use 3-period moving average for smoothing.
- If sentiment is high (≥0.75) and price is trending up, model often overreacts; apply downward bias of 3–7% to avoid overconfidence in bullish sentiment.
- When sentiment is mixed or volatile (alternating 0.33–0.75), model exhibits mean-reversion bias; align forecast with 10-day rolling mean of past 30d.
- If true outcome shows early downward correction (first 5–7 days of 30d), model often lags; adjust forecast to match first 3–5 days of true trend, then apply sentiment-weighted decay.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if sentiment is negative or neutral, model tends to underestimate; add 1–3% upward bias to compensate for sentiment drag.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “0.00” or extreme negativity, model underestimates; increase forecast by 5–10% to account for suppressed market behavior.
